title: Guru Arjan close
hookLine: poet, builder, editor and martyr: four names for one life

cards: Four job titles, one life: poet, builder, editor, martyr.

On a résumé they'd look like four different people: one at a desk with a pen, one on a building site with mud on his hands, one sorting pages by lamplight, one standing firm when the powerful came for him.
In Sikh memory they're all the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan. Today, a step back to look at the whole man, and ask what ties the four together.

teach.b: The poet first. Guru Arjan wrote the Bavan Akhri, the alphabet that ends in grace. He wrote Sukhmani, a name often explained as the jewel of peace, and read for comfort.
He wrote tera keeaa meethaa laagai: what You do seems sweet to me. The builder. At Amritsar, around the pool his father began, the Harmandir Sahib rose.

teach.h: THE BUILDER: DOORS ON EVERY SIDE.
teach.b: Tradition says it was built with doors on every side, open to anyone from any direction. He sang that the Lord Himself stood to finish the saints' work.
The editor: Gurus and bhagats, chosen carefully, gathered into one volume. And the martyr. History records that he was arrested under the Mughal emperor Jahangir and died in Lahore.

Sikh tradition remembers torture, and remembers him meeting it without bitterness; Gurdwara Dera Sahib in Lahore marks the place tradition gives for his death. In the telling, that sweet line comes back.
So what ties the four together?

teach.h: A PLACE FOR OTHERS TO STAND.
teach.b: Each time, he made a place for other people to stand. A song you can rest inside. A pool and a building you can walk into from any side.
A book you can bow to and read.
And an example of faith that held under the worst kind of pressure. He didn't build for himself.
You met the chhabeel back on day one hundred fifty: on his martyrdom day, Sikhs set up stands by the road and hand cool, sweet water to anyone passing, whoever they are.
A sweet drink for a stranger, in memory of a man who called God's will sweet.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Arjan on his martyrdom day with kirtan, readings of his hymns such as Sukhmani, and chhabeel, roadside stands serving cool sweetened water to anyone passing.

games.q: you're building a holy place, and you want anyone to feel they can come in. where do you put the doors?
o: one gate, facing the holiest direction.
a gate for the faithful only.
games.why: tradition says the Harmandir was built with doors on every side, so anyone could come in from any direction.

practice: Look around your life for something other people stand in, a family meal, a kind group chat, a shelf at work everyone uses, a song you sing to a child, and choose one. Picture it a little more open, like a door on another side.
Hold that picture, and if you pray, remember Waheguru on each breath in.

wordCard.voice: Guru Arjan close. Poet, builder, editor and martyr: one life spent making places, in words and in stone, for other people to stand. Today's word.

orig.note: martyr, a witness; Sikhs honor Guru Arjan as a shaheed.

carryVoice: Your line: poet and builder. Words and walls, both built for someone else. Until tomorrow.
